children.translated_text: *<s>Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā</s> (Examination of the Theist's Doctrine)

children.text: , 81-85 einen Text Jitāris ediert, der im Kolophon als
idānīm ārhatamataṃ vicāryate; - ihāmī digambarāḥ dravyaparyāyarūpeṇa utpattisthitipralayātmakaṃ bhāvagrāmaṃ varṇayanti |...

Im vorliegenden Konvolut findet sich nun ein Text, der eine ganz ähnliche Struktur hat, dessen Titel uns aber nicht erhalten ist. Er umfaßt die Folios IIB|9; IIA|9; IIB|6; IIA|6; IIB|11; IIA|11; IIB|10; IIA|10; IIB|12; IIA|12; (Schluß fehlt). Entsprechend der

children.translated_text: Now the doctrine of the theists (<s>Īśvaravādins</s>) is examined.
Here, these <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others [claim that] trees and such —
all effects — are made by <s>Īśvara</s> (God).
So they declare.
But what is their means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for that?
Inference (<s>anumāna</s>). For thus:
Whatever is an effect is seen to be inseparable from a maker,
just as the effect of a pot and the like.
And similarly
trees and such, which are the subject of dispute, [are effects] —

children.text: yaś cāsau kartā sa bhagavān Īśvara iti |
children.translated_text: and the maker of these is the blessed <s>Īśvara</s> — so [they say].
then the inference that trees and such are caused by an intelligent agent, based on seeing their effect-nature,
would be valid.
However, this very pervasion is impossible
to ascertain.

children.text: tathā hi puruṣasya vyāpāram antareṇāpy upa
children.translated_text: For thus: even without the activity of a person,
grass and such arise —
such things are observed. How then could one who acts with deliberation determine that all effects are of human origin?

children.text: pūrvakāriṇā sarvaṃ kāryaṃ pauruṣeyam iti niścīyeta |

children.translated_text: To this we say: If all effects were of well-established pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) with being caused by an intelligent agent,
is observed,
and those effects whose origination is observed [with human activity] —
all those, grass and such
and mountains and such,

children.text: ca pakṣīkṛtā eva | na ca pakṣīkṛte vyāpti
children.translated_text: are included in the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣa</s>). And when something is included in the thesis-subject, the ascertainment of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>)
is possible in some cases —
because the pervader being imperceptible

children.text: vyāpter grahītum aśakyatvāt kvacic ca vyāptigrāhiṇa eva pra
children.translated_text: makes the pervasion impossible to grasp [in some cases], and because in some cases the very means of valid knowledge that grasps pervasion
is unestablished — [otherwise] inference would have no entry at all.
Therefore, just as
in a kitchen and such, the pervasion of smoke with fire is cognized,
so too here,
in pots and such, the pervasion of effects with being caused by an intelligent agent is cognized.

children.text: yathā vānyatra gṛhītavyāptikaḥ puruṣaḥ parvatādau dhūmadarśa
children.translated_text: And just as elsewhere, a person who has grasped the pervasion infers fire on a mountain and such from seeing smoke
similarly, from seeing effect-nature in grass and such, one would infer a maker

children.text: rtāram anumimīta iti na kiṃcid anupapannaṃ nāma |
children.translated_text: — there is nothing at all that is unjustified.
Objection: Those for which origination without human activity

children.text: tad asat | tathā hi puruṣavyāpāram antareṇāpi tṛṇādīn

children.translated_text: the world does not ascertain the very pervasion that all effects are preceded by a person.
This has [already] been stated.
Thereupon, by this one who is deaf at heart,

children.text: karṇahṛdayena tṛṇādayo 'smābhiḥ sarva eva pakṣīkṛtā iti bru
children.translated_text: saying 'grass and such have all been included by us in the thesis-subject' — we do not understand what resolution has been given.

children.text: vatā kiṃ nāma samādhānaṃ dattam iti na pratīmaḥ | yadi hi dhūmo
children.translated_text: For if smoke were seen arising even without fire,

children.text: vahnim antareṇāpy upajāyamāno dṛśyeta kiṃ tasya kaścit tato
children.translated_text: would anyone ascertain its pervasion with that [fire]?
That is wrong. For thus: observing grass and such arising even without human activity,
consider: that [maker] is an unseen, supersensory
special person.
Therefore, even though the production of grass and such is preceded by his activity,
it is not cognized as such.
And the non-apprehension of what is unseen does not establish the absence of the thing. Therefore,

children.text: yady api tṛṇādayaḥ puruṣapūrvakā na pratīyante tathāpi na teṣām
children.translated_text: even though grass and such are not cognized as preceded by a person, still it is not [established] that they are
definitely not of human origin, so that there would be failure to grasp the pervasion.
[Opponent:] Well then,

children.text: etad apy asat | yato na tāvad iha puruṣavyāpārapūrvakatā

children.translated_text: cognized for grass and such. And whether it is not cognized because the person is unseen
or because he is nonexistent —
let it not be cognized.
What is the use of investigating this?
In any case, someone who does not see any
effect preceded by a person [recognizes] under-pervasion (<s>avyāpti</s>),
and someone ascertains [that not] all effects
[are pervaded] by a person. And when pervasion is not ascertained,
how can there even be talk of
inference?
This too is wrong. For it is the case that the precedence of human activity is not

children.text: syād etat | yadi na buddhimatpūrvakaṃ kāryaṃ ghaṭādikam
api tathābhūtaṃ na syāt | akāraṇāt sakṛd apy anutpatteḥ |
children.translated_text: then it would not be so [i.e., preceded by a maker]. Since what has no cause never arises even once,

children.text: tasmād ekam api kāryaṃ puruṣakāraṇakaṃ pratiyan viśeṣābhā
children.translated_text: therefore, one who cognizes even a single effect as having a personal cause, due to the absence of a distinguishing feature
ascertains every effect as preceded by an intelligent being.

children.text: yathā mahānase vahnihetukaṃ dhūmam upalabhamānaḥ sarvam eva
children.translated_text: Just as one who observes smoke in a kitchen to be caused by fire
determines all smoke to be caused by that [fire].
[Opponent:] It may be [argued] thus: If the effect of pots and such were also not preceded by an intelligent being,
For a different
kind of effect indeed —
pots and such — is seen as having a human cause.
And this [other kind]
— slender trees and such — is different. The designation 'effect'

children.text: eva samānaṃ pralāpaḥ | tato vyāptipratītikāle pratikṣiptam
children.translated_text: alone is common — [the similarity is merely] verbal. Therefore, at the time of cognizing the pervasion, [the latter] was already rejected

children.text: evedṛśam | na hi vahnivyāptaṃ dhūmaṃ pratipadyamāna
children.translated_text: as such. For no one who ascertains smoke as pervaded by fire
also ascertains [as pervaded by fire] smoke depicted in a painting, merely because of the commonality of being
designated by the word 'smoke.'
This too is not right, because the very absence of a distinguishing feature is unestablished.

children.text: nanu ghaṭādikam api kāraṇe sati bhāvāt
ucyate | tarvādikam api sati kāraṇe bhavat kāryavyavahārayogyam
children.translated_text: and trees and such too, existing when a cause exists, are fit for the designation 'effect.'

children.text: iti kāryatvena vivādāspadībhūtetarayor aviśeṣād ekatra buddhi
children.translated_text: Since the two — which have become the subject of dispute on account of their effect-nature — are not different, the fact that one [set, pots etc.,]
is preceded by an intelligent being
leads to the cognition that the same holds everywhere.
Objection: Pots and such are also called 'effects' because they exist when the cause exists,
for smoke-effects
would likewise yield the inference that all effects are caused by
fire —
such reasoning would also apply to the fool (<s>devānāṃpriya</s>).
To this we say: Since there is no difference between smoke and non-smoke [i.e., other effects] in being effects, the cognition of fire-causation

children.text: atha manyase na kāryamātraṃ vahnimātravyāptaṃ pratipannaṃ
kiṃ tu kāryaviśeṣo dhūma iti tata eva tasyānumānaṃ na kārya
children.translated_text: but smoke is a specific kind of effect' — then for that very reason the inference is from smoke [specifically], not from effect-nature
in general.
If you think: 'Not all effects are cognized as pervaded by fire in general,
cognized as pervaded by fire, just as [you claim it is] pervaded by a person?

children.text: api na pratīyata ity etad evocyate | tatrāpi hi śakyam etad
children.translated_text: This is precisely what is being said. For there too one could state this:
'If any
effect were not preceded by fire,

children.text: dhūmo 'py agnipūrvako na syāt | akāraṇasya sakṛd apy
children.translated_text: smoke too would not be preceded by fire — since what is not a cause never produces even once.'
Why then is not all effect-nature

children.text: atha kāryāntaram agnim antareṇāpi jāyamānaṃ dṛṣṭam iti na

children.translated_text: not all effects are pervaded by fire.
But then: another effect is seen arising even without fire — therefore

children.text: tṛṇādikam api puruṣam antareṇa jāyamānaṃ dṛṣṭam
children.translated_text: grass and such too are seen arising without a person,
therefore the pervasion of all effects by a person cannot be cognized.
If so,
to be preceded by that [cause],

children.text: upalabhyate tādṛśam eva tadvyāptam avadhāryata iti kāryamātrād
children.translated_text: only that kind is determined to be pervaded by that [cause] — [and so] the inference is not from effect-nature in general.
[Opponent:] But whatever kind of effect is observed through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>)

children.text: evaṃ tarhi yādṛśam eva kāryam anvayavyatirekābhyā
ruṣapūrvakam upalabhyate tādṛśam eva tadvyāptam avadhāryata
children.translated_text: to be preceded by a person, only that kind is determined to be pervaded by that [person],
and therefore there is no inference of a person from effect-nature in general.
And it is a different kind of effect —
pots and such — that is observed to conform to the positive and negative concomitance with a person.
This must be acknowledged
even unwillingly by the opponent...

children.translated_text: from those who do not perceive activity
[there is] the dissimilarity of trees and such from [things] born of an intelligent agent's design.
And since, in the absence of being of a different kind from what has become the subject of dispute,
like a temple seen in an empty

children.text: dṛṣṭasya devakulāder iva vṛkṣāder api nāsmadādivilakṣaṇakartṛ
children.translated_text: city, even for trees and such, the inference of a maker different from ourselves
would not necessarily follow.
If so, then whatever kind of effect is observed through positive and negative concomitance
If [you say] the dissimilarity of the maker of trees and such from ourselves and the like is stated precisely because of [his] being unseen,
For the proponents of <s>Īśvara</s> as cause do not accept that the difference between the maker of pots and the maker of trees lies merely
in being seen
versus unseen,
since unseen [beings] such as <s>piśācas</s> (demons) and the like can exist. Nor can it

children.text: śācāder adṛśyasya saṃbhavāt | na ca ya eva vṛkṣādikārī puruṣo
children.translated_text: be said that the very person who makes trees and such and is unseen to us is <s>Īśvara</s>,
for their intent is that <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) is a special person who is skilled in creating the universe,
who knows the ultimate reality of all things,
— and not [merely any unseen agent]. Moreover, even if the precedence of an unseen
maker is established, the single-maker status even of trees of the same kind

children.text: ekakartṛkatā sidhyati | prāg eva nagaranadīparvatādīnām ekā
children.translated_text: is not established — much less for cities, rivers, mountains, and such, which are entirely
of mutually different kinds.
For even of pots and such, which have a visible maker,
a single
maker is not cognized.
that too is not reasonable.
'We ourselves know the range of power of beings like ourselves. And even a capable person such as ourselves
cannot construct
these mountains and such. Therefore, the one who fashions mountains and such,
being established [as a maker], is established as
necessarily different from ourselves and the like.'
One may think:
For the following
is the topic here: even one who advocates for <s>Īśvara</s> must necessarily acknowledge
the dissimilarity of trees and such from pots and such.
How could these [trees etc.], which are experienced as different from the products of other persons,

children.text: kāryebhyo viśeṣam anubhavantaḥ katham amī tadvilakṣaṇena kartrā
children.translated_text: be established as made by a maker different from them

children.text: kṛtāḥ sādhyerann iti | tato yady ayam idānīm asmadādyatiśā
children.translated_text: [yet similar in kind]? Therefore, if this [opponent] now, in the hope of establishing a person surpassing ourselves,
states the dissimilarity of trees and such from our products by virtue of their being
impossible for us to create,
then

children.text: siddham eṣām anyādṛśatvam | siddhe cānyādṛśatve na ghaṭādīnāṃ
children.translated_text: the different-nature of these [trees etc.] is established. And once their different-nature is established, the pervasion that 'all effects are of human origin' —
established from the human-origin status of effects like pots —
is not established, and so a water-offering must be given [in farewell] to the proof of <s>Īśvara</s>.
The fool (<s>devānāṃpriya</s>), prone to forgetfulness, fails to notice the topic [of discussion].
The pervasion with a person, however, since he is unseen,
is not contradicted by
perception in the case of grass and such.
This too was stated by the <s>Nyāya</s>-teacher (<s>Nyāyācārya</s>).
[Opponent:] But because it is contradicted by perception, not all effects are cognized as pervaded by fire.
the pervasion of all effects with fire
[that which] grasps it — that <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge)
or not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. If

children.text: tāvat tat pramāṇaṃ kathaṃ tasya pramā
children.translated_text: it is indeed a <s>pramāṇa</s>, how can its invali-
da-
tion by another <s>pramāṇa</s>
[be established]?

children.text: athāpramāṇaṃ dhūmasyāpi tena vahnivyāptir aśakyā sādhayitum
children.translated_text: But if it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, then even the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) of smoke with fire cannot be established by it.
If [one argues that] it establishes the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) of the effect of smoke with fire — since there is no difference insofar as being an effect is concerned,
why should it not establish [the concomitance] of other [effects] too? Thus enters the suspicion of an irremediable difficulty.
For here there are two alternatives: if
If [one argues that] only a specific
effect
is inseparable from fire,
then there is no
determination that an effect of a different kind from that
is pervaded by fire.
is inseparable from a person (<s>puruṣa</s>) — so there is no
determination that [an effect] of a different kind is pervaded by a person. Thus the objection regarding the invalida-
tion or non-invalidation by perception
is not stronger [than our position]. The inability of us and the like
is not [evidence of] the truth [of the theistic position].
If the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) were [established] by observation and non-observation
of <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proven) and <s>sādhana</s> (the means of proof),
[and they are] without obstruction,
then it would not be appropriate to describe the invariable concomitance of mere effects with having a person (<s>puruṣa</s>) as their antecedent
— it would not be proper to describe
[such a <s>vyāpti</s>], because even in the absence of observing a person's activity, the arising of grass
and the like
is observed. If [the <s>vyāpti</s> is] based on a necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) —

children.text: tadāpi na kāryamātrasya puruṣapūrvakatayā vyāptir upavarṇa
children.translated_text: even then, it is not appropriate to describe the invariable concomitance of mere effects with having a person as their antece-

children.text: yituṃ yuktā | tasyaiva pratibandhasiddher asiddher ity alaṃ
children.translated_text: dent, because the establishment of that very necessary connection is itself unestablished. Enough
of much speaking.
Therefore, this stands established: this [world] is without a creator.
